name: Brainmaxxing

card.summary: Applying the looksmaxxing "-maxxing" mindset to cognition, with sleep, exercise, diet, supplements and study routines that members hope will raise focus, mood and drive, which they link to confidence and a better-kept appearance.
card.note: Some forum stacks involve prescription stimulants and unregulated nootropics; electrical-stimulation ideas for height or growth have no published support.

quick.overview:
Brainmaxxing is internet slang for deliberately optimising intelligence and mental performance, borrowing the "-maxxing" suffix from looksmaxxing. On looksmax.org it sits beside appearance topics because members connect a sharper, calmer, more confident mind with how they present themselves and follow through on routines.

Practices range from ordinary habits such as sleep, exercise and diet to nootropic supplements, prescription medicines used off-label, and fringe ideas like using electrical stimulation to influence growth. Published research on cognitive enhancement in healthy adults is mixed and task-specific, and none of it addresses appearance.
quick.how: In forum threads, people describe "stacks" of supplements, regular meditation, limits on gaming and sugar, exercise and sleep routines, and sometimes prescription stimulants. Some posts propose transcranial current or TENS devices. Results are reported anecdotally over weeks.
quick.risks: Nootropics and off-label prescription drugs can cause insomnia, headaches, stomach upset and dependence, and long-term effects are poorly understood. Reviewers also note that gains from supplements and brain-training apps tend to be small and limited to practised tasks. Stimulating electrodes at home carries its own risks.

lead: Brainmaxxing (also brainsmaxxing, or "brainmax") is a slang term for unconventional or intensive efforts to raise intelligence and cognitive performance. It uses the "-maxxing" suffix that began in online forums such as Lookism.net around 2014 to 2015 and spread from looksmaxxing to other areas, a pattern also noted in Wikipedia's account of the suffix's origins [5][9].

On looksmax.org the term appears in threads about nootropic stacks, recovery from depression, and the idea that mental state shows in demeanour and confidence. One poster recovering from a poor surgery outcome and a depressive episode laid out a plan involving meditation, reduced gaming and sugar, and stimulant medication to rebuild memory [3]. Others describe a spice compound as shaping the self-assured behaviour they attribute to certain groups [2], or propose TENS and transcranial stimulation for growth and height goals [1].

Mainstream coverage has also adopted the word: a 2026 New York Times opinion column titled "Forget About Looksmaxxing. Brainmaxxing Is the Real Rage" is cited in a T Nation discussion [4]. Research on nootropics, cognitive training and lifestyle habits exists as a general field, but no study has tested brainmaxxing as a looksmaxxing practice.

chain: Better sleep, mood, focus and drive
More consistent skincare, training and grooming habits
angle.text: Members treat cognitive upkeep as the foundation that lets them keep appearance routines going and carry themselves with more confidence. The link to how someone looks is indirect and runs through habits and demeanour.

infobox: Offshoot of the "-maxxing" suffix from looksmaxxing forums (2010s)
Sleep, exercise, diet, nootropics, meditation, study

paras: The term refers to optimising cognition rather than appearance. Grokipedia's overview describes it as often involving "out of pocket" habits such as learning obscure facts alongside more standard routines [5]. The suffix itself derives from the gaming concept of min-maxing [5].

Commonly listed methods include sleep of about eight hours, exercise such as zone 2 cardio and high-intensity intervals, diets rich in fish-derived DHA or low in carbohydrate, intermittent fasting, brain-training apps, and nootropics such as piracetam, modafinil, ginkgo and bacopa [5]. The same overview reports that gains from these methods are modest, mixed or limited to practised tasks, and that reviews find no clear short-term cognitive benefit from intermittent fasting in healthy adults [5].

Forum posters add routines like daily meditation with or without binaural beats and reduced pornography, gaming and sugar intake, aimed at restoring "dopamine sensitivity" [3]. One thread suggests the neurosurgical drug cerebrolysin as a recovery aid [3].

A looksmax.org thread titled "Brainmaxxing and heightmaxxing?" argues that frequency-based devices such as TENS or transcranial current stimulation could influence the hypothalamus and pituitary, or stimulate jawbone growth when electrodes are placed on the skin [1]. The poster acknowledges that growth is regulated by complex biochemical signals that are hard to mimic with simple stimulation, and a reply claims height gains from similar techniques [1]. Grokipedia notes that tDCS results are mixed in cognition studies [5]. No published trial has tested these devices for height or jaw growth.

No studies found on brainmaxxing as a practice. A series of Russian randomised trials tested a succinic-acid-based drug sold under the name Brainmax for post-COVID fatigue, mild cognitive impairment and stroke recovery [6][7][8]. These concern a pharmaceutical product that shares the name and are unrelated to the slang term.

timeline.event: The "-maxxing" suffix appears on forums such as Lookism.net and then 4chan [5].
A New York Times opinion column on brainmaxxing is discussed on T Nation [4].

lore.intro: Brainmaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix supplement stacks, mood recovery plans and speculative theories [1][2][3].

claims.claim: Electrical stimulation (TENS/tCDS) can influence growth and height
claims.believers: The original poster argues that stimulating the hypothalamus, pituitary or electrodes over the jaw may help growth, and a reply reports going from 183 to 194 cm with similar techniques [1].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested electrical stimulation for height or bone growth; research on tDCS concerns cognition with mixed results [5].

claims.claim: Curcumin shapes confident, assertive behaviour by inhibiting monoamine oxidase A
claims.believers: A thread proposes that curcumin's MAO-A inhibition produces "warrior gene"-like behaviour, and some replies find the theory plausible while others call it overgeneralised [2].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this claim as framed.

claims.claim: A structured stack of habits and supplements can rebuild cognition after depression
claims.believers: A poster outlines meditation, reduced gaming and sugar, and stimulant medication as a recovery plan [3].
claims.experts: Overviews note that nootropics and cognitive training show limited, task-specific gains in healthy people [5].
